assessment.nobel_worthiness: Founded modern political economics by applying rigorous formal and empirical methods to constitutions, electoral rules, state capacity and fiscal policy. It explains how political institutions shape economic policy and outcomes. It is close to the institutions-and-prosperity theme the Committee recognised in 2024, but covers different mechanisms: electoral systems, forms of government and fiscal capacity.
assessment.attribution: Persson and Tabellini developed the constitutional and electoral-rule research programme (Political Economics, 2000). Besley and Persson are central to the state-capacity and fiscal-capacity literature. The three-person limit forces a choice, and Besley's contributions beyond state capacity are also substantial. Persson is a Stockholm-based scholar, so disclosed ties are plausible; this is noted, not adjudicated.
assessment.maturity: Core results date from the 1990s and 2000s and are replicated, cited widely and taught across economics and political science. The field is well established, and the timing is ripe.
uncertainties: Whether the Committee prefers a political-economy prize this soon after 2024.
Allocation of credit among Persson, Tabellini and Besley, and the relative weight of Besley's separate work.
My own field is political science, which could bias my sense of this area's importance. I rely on common criteria.
Possible institutional or personal ties of Persson to the Committee; I cannot verify them.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The China shock and task-based analyses of technology and trade changed how economists understand the local labour-market, distributional and political effects of globalisation and automation. The work is empirically credible, policy-relevant and has broad influence across fields, including political economy.
assessment.attribution: Autor, Dorn and Hanson are jointly credited with the China-shock papers and Autor with the task-based framework and polarisation work. Lawrence Katz's earlier skill-biased technical change work is also credited to the candidate but would exceed the three-name limit. The task-model lineage also involves other scholars outside this list, notably Acemoglu, who is already a laureate.
assessment.maturity: Key papers date from 2003 to 2013 and have had over a decade of replication, extension and debate. The magnitude of effects and long-run adjustment remain debated but the core finding is robust.
uncertainties: Whether the Committee views the contribution as a body of empirical findings rather than a conceptual or methodological breakthrough.
Overlap with the Acemoglu-Autor task framework and the choice among Autor, Hanson, Dorn and Katz.
Continuing debate about the persistence and size of trade-shock effects.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Their 1997 model of credit cycles shows how collateral constraints amplify and propagate shocks. It is a foundational mechanism in macro-finance and was central to the post-2008 understanding of financial crises. It has strong theoretical depth and wide use in policy models.
assessment.attribution: Kiyotaki and Moore are the clear originators of the collateral-constraint credit-cycle model. Bernanke, Gertler and Gilchrist's financial accelerator is a parallel contribution, and Bernanke is already a laureate. Restricting the proposal to the original pair keeps the credit well defined.
assessment.maturity: The key paper is nearly thirty years old and has been extended in many directions. The post-2008 empirical vindication adds weight.
uncertainties: How the Committee balances Kiyotaki-Moore against the Bernanke-Gertler-Gilchrist financial accelerator.
Whether the model is seen as a stand-alone Nobel-level contribution or a part of a broader macro-finance prize.
Moderate empirical identification of the mechanism.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The BLP demand-estimation framework and dynamic-industry structural estimation are among the most widely used empirical tools in industrial organisation, antitrust and trade. They enable credible estimation of demand and market power with differentiated products, and the framework has become standard practice in applied work.
assessment.attribution: Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes created the BLP method, and Berry's 1994 inversion is a key step. Pakes also has separate work on dynamic games (Ericson-Pakes) and on estimation. Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin are also credited but their contributions are more distinct and would not fit within three names.
assessment.maturity: BLP dates from 1995 and has been used for decades with extensive methodological refinements. The work is mature and well confirmed by use.
uncertainties: Whether the Committee treats methodological tools as sufficient on their own for the prize.
Credit division with Bresnahan and others in the structural-IO tradition.
Concerns about the sensitivity of structural estimates to modelling assumptions.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Used population-scale administrative data to measure intergenerational mobility, neighbourhood effects and the causal effects of place and policy. It reshaped public economics and policy debate and set new data and identification standards. The impact is large and still growing.
assessment.attribution: Chetty leads the programme and is the dominant figure, while Hendren (neighbourhood and exposure effects) and Friedman (teacher value-added and tax data) are major co-authors. Katz's work on Moving to Opportunity is also credited but would exceed the limit. Collaborative credit is spread across a large team.
assessment.maturity: Core mobility papers date from 2014 onward, so the work is relatively recent and the long-run confirmation is still emerging. Replication and external validity are still being tested.
uncertainties: Relative recency of the main results may argue for waiting.
Allocation of credit within a large collaboration and among Chetty, Hendren, Friedman and Katz.
Debate about causal interpretation of some neighbourhood-effect estimates.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Melitz 2003 model of heterogeneous firms and selection transformed trade theory and empirics. It explains exporter premia, within-industry reallocation and a new channel for gains from trade. It is foundational for a generation of research in trade and macro.
assessment.attribution: Melitz is the clear originator. Helpman's contributions on firm heterogeneity, trade and the organisation of firms are substantial, while Redding's work on quantitative spatial and trade models extends the framework. Krugman's earlier prize covered new trade theory, which affects how the Committee will see novelty.
assessment.maturity: Over two decades old, empirically tested and integrated into the standard toolkit. It is well established and a plausible time for recognition.
uncertainties: Overlap with Krugman's earlier prize on new trade theory and with the quantitative trade candidate B001.
Whether Helpman or Redding is the better second name.
Robustness of some welfare implications to alternative assumptions about distributions.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Showed that misallocation of resources across firms can account for a sizeable share of cross-country income gaps. It established a quantitative and measurement-based framework in growth and development with wide influence on productivity research and policy.
assessment.attribution: Hsieh and Klenow (2009) are the clear core. Restuccia and Rogerson (2008) developed a parallel framework, but Rogerson is not credited here, which complicates attribution. Credit for the broader misallocation literature is diffuse.
assessment.maturity: About fifteen to eighteen years old, with heavy use and extensions. Debate continues about measurement error in the productivity distortions.
uncertainties: Sensitivity of results to measurement error and to model assumptions.
Missing credit for Rogerson in this list.
Whether the Committee views this as conceptual or primarily measurement.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Built long-run historical series on top incomes and wealth from tax data, which transformed the empirical study of inequality and brought it to the centre of economics and public debate. The data contribution is major, and the interpretive and policy claims are more contested.
assessment.attribution: Piketty and Saez are the central authors of the top-income series (2003). Zucman is credited for offshore wealth and later distributional accounts. Saez also appears in candidate B014 on optimal taxation, creating overlap across candidates.
assessment.maturity: Core series date from 2000 to 2003, and the field is extensive. The theoretical interpretation, such as r > g, is disputed.
uncertainties: Contested theoretical claims and methodological critiques of the wealth and income estimates.
Whether the Committee treats a data and measurement contribution as sufficient.
Overlap of Saez with other candidates and the question of Zucman's inclusion.
